opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's an interesting question, because when people hear "reasoning" they often think of math problems or puzzles. For robots doing everyday tasks, it looks a bit different.

One kind is breaking a task into steps. If you ask a robot to clean up a kitchen, it has to figure out that this means putting dishes in the sink, wiping the counter, and throwing away trash, and then work through those pieces in a sensible order. Language models are pretty good at that kind of high-level decomposition, and we've found it really helps when a robot can, in a sense, talk itself through what it should do next.

Another kind is more physical and closer to common sense. If I'm folding a shirt and one sleeve is crumpled underneath, I need to recognize that and flatten it out before I keep going. Or if I'm grabbing a cup that's full, I need to keep it upright. That isn't something you would write out in words, but it's still reasoning about the state of the world and what will happen when you act on it.

Then there's reasoning about failure and recovery, which I think is underrated. Robots make mistakes all the time. They miss a grasp or knock something over. The ability to notice that something went wrong and adjust, instead of blindly continuing with the original plan, is a big part of what makes a system actually useful in a messy home or office.

Finally, there's reasoning about the person. If someone says "I'm thirsty," the robot should figure out that they probably want a drink and maybe which one. That means interpreting vague instructions and filling in the gaps the way a person would.

What's exciting is that these don't have to be separate modules anymore. With vision-language-action models, some of that high-level semantic reasoning can carry over from web-scale pretraining, while the low-level physical understanding comes from robot data. The open question is how to get those to work together smoothly, so the robot thinks hard when it needs to and acts quickly and fluidly when it doesn't.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different kinds, and they operate at pretty different levels. The first is what you might call high-level task reasoning: if I ask a robot to clean up the kitchen, it needs to break that down. Put the dishes in the sink, wipe the counter, throw away the trash. That's the kind of thing language models are actually quite good at now, because it's mostly common sense about how the world works and what "clean up" means.

The second kind is much lower level, and honestly it's where a lot of the difficulty is. It's reasoning about the physical world: if I grasp this cup from the side, is it going to slip? If I push this drawer, is something going to fall? That's not really something you can get from reading the internet. It requires grounding in physical experience, and a lot of it may not be reasoning in the explicit, verbal sense at all. It's more like intuition that comes from having interacted with objects a lot.

And then there's a middle layer that I think is underappreciated, which is reasoning about failure and recovery. Robots in the real world mess up constantly. The cup slips, the drawer sticks. A useful robot needs to notice that, figure out what went wrong, and try something different, rather than just replaying the plan. Humans do this effortlessly, and it's a big part of what makes everyday tasks hard for robots.

One thing I'd add is that I'm somewhat skeptical of the idea that robots need to do a lot of explicit, step-by-step reasoning for most everyday tasks. When you load a dishwasher, you're not deliberating. So I think the goal is to use explicit reasoning where it helps, for planning and for handling novel situations, and to let a lot of the rest be learned directly from data and experience.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few different kinds. One is physical reasoning: if I push this object, where is it going to go? If I pick it up this way, is it going to slip? That’s useful even for something as simple as putting a cup in a dishwasher.

Then there’s reasoning over longer sequences of actions. If you’re making dinner, you need to figure out what to do first, what can happen in parallel, and whether you have the ingredients. And there’s reasoning about people: when someone asks you to clean up the kitchen, what do they actually want you to do? What should you put away, and what should you leave out?

The interesting thing is that all of this has to connect back to perception and action. You can make a sensible plan, but then you try to open a drawer and it’s stuck. The robot needs to use that observation to reconsider what to do next. So it’s not just reasoning before acting; it’s reasoning as you interact with the world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few different kinds. There’s physical reasoning: if I push this object, where is it going to go? If I pick it up this way, is it going to slip? And then there’s reasoning over longer sequences of actions. If I want to cook a meal, what do I need to do first, and what depends on something else being done?

There’s also reasoning about people and what they actually want. If someone asks a robot to clean up the kitchen, that leaves a lot unspecified. What should go in the dishwasher? What should stay on the counter? When should it ask a question?

The interesting thing is that all of these have to connect to perception and action. The robot doesn’t get a complete description of the world. It might need to open a drawer to see what’s inside, or try picking something up to learn whether it’s too heavy. So useful reasoning isn’t just making a plan up front. It’s figuring out what to do next as you act and get new information.
